units.t: Commonly Confused Words.
Part one. Affect or effect.
Some pairs of English words are almost designed to trip us up.
They sound alike, or nearly alike, and they live in the same kinds of sentences.
In this lesson, we'll untangle five of the most common pairs, with a simple memory trick for each.
If you're driving, there's no need to picture the letters.
Just listen, and the tricks will do the work.
Let's start with the pair that catches out nearly everyone.
Affect and effect.
Affect is spelled A, F, F, E, C, T.
Effect is spelled E, F, F, E, C, T.
Here they are in one everyday sentence.
The wet weather will affect the footy tonight, and the effect could be a very muddy game.
In most everyday sentences, affect is a verb.
It's something you do.
To affect something means to influence it or change it.
Effect, on the other hand, is usually a noun.
It's a thing, the result of a change.
So the rain affects the game, and the muddy pitch is the effect.
There's a popular memory trick for this, and it's a bird.
RAVEN.
Remember, Affect is a Verb, Effect is a Noun.
Here's a second trick that some people find even easier.
A is for action, and affect is the action.
E is for end result, and effect is the end result.
And here's a quick test you can do in your head.
If you can put the word the in front of it, as in, the effect, you almost certainly want effect with an E.
If you can swap in the word influence, you probably want affect with an A.
Now, English being English, there are exceptions.
Effect can sometimes be a verb, meaning to bring something about.
If a new manager effects change, she makes change happen.
If a new manager affects change, she influences a change that's already underway.
You'll mostly see that in formal writing, and it's worth knowing so it doesn't throw you.
Affect can sometimes be a noun too, but mainly in psychology.
Doctors and psychologists talk about a person's affect, meaning the emotion they show on the outside.
In that case it's said with the stress at the front, AFF-ect.
For everyday life, though, RAVEN will get you through almost every time.
Let's try two quick ones in your head.
In each sentence, I'll say the word blank where the missing word goes.
First sentence.
Her new shift pattern had a big blank on her sleep.
Which word fills the blank?
It's a thing, a result, so it's effect with an E.
Second sentence.
The long commute started to blank his mood.
This time it's an action, something being influenced, so it's affect with an A.
Easy once you've got the bird on your side.
Part two. Fewer or less.
Our second pair appears on supermarket signs all over the world.
Fewer and less.
Fewer is spelled F, E, W, E, R.
Less is spelled L, E, S, S.
Here's an example that uses both.
There were fewer cars on the road this morning, so there was less traffic.
The traditional rule goes like this.
Use fewer for things you can count one by one.
Fewer cars, fewer people, fewer emails.
Use less for things you measure as an amount, rather than count.
Less traffic, less water, less noise.
A handy trick is to ask yourself, could I put a number in front of it?
You can say three cars, so it's fewer cars.
You can't say three traffics, so it's less traffic.
Here's the classic battleground.
That sign at the express checkout that says ten items or less.
Strictly by the traditional rule, it should be ten items or fewer, because items can be counted.
In 2008, the British supermarket chain Tesco changed its signs after complaints from a group called the Plain English Campaign.
Their solution was clever.
They sidestepped the whole argument by writing, up to ten items.
But here's something interesting.
The rule itself is younger than you might think.
English speakers have used less with countable things since the time of King Alfred, well over a thousand years ago.
The fewer rule is usually traced to a writer called Robert Baker, in 1770.
In a book on English usage, he said that fewer would do better than less when speaking of a number.
He was only giving his personal preference, but later grammar books turned it into a firm rule.
There are also some sensible exceptions that even careful writers accept.
We use less with money, time, distance and weight, because we think of them as amounts rather than separate units.
So it's less than $20, not fewer than $20.
It's less than five kilometres to the shops, and less than two hours to Canberra.
And it's perfectly natural to say one less thing to worry about.
The takeaway is simple.
If you can count them individually, fewer is the safe choice.
If it's an amount, or money, time or distance, reach for less.
Part three. Three more quick pairs.
Our third pair is complement and compliment.
Complement with an E is spelled C, O, M, P, L, E, M, E, N, T.
Compliment with an I is spelled C, O, M, P, L, I, M, E, N, T.
Here they are together.
The waiter paid me a compliment on my choice of wine, and said it would complement the lamb perfectly.
Complement with an E means to complete something, or go well with it.
Notice that complement and complete share the same first six letters, C, O, M, P, L, E.
That's your trick.
A complement completes.
A good sauce complements a dish.
A new team member might complement the skills already there.
Compliment with an I is a kind remark.
The trick here is, I like compliments.
There's one small twist.
Complimentary with an I also means free, as in complimentary tea and coffee in the waiting room.
That's because a free gift was originally a kind of politeness, a compliment from the business.
Complementary with an E means things that go together, like complementary colours, or complementary medicine alongside regular treatment.
Our fourth pair is stationary and stationery.
Stationary with an A is spelled S, T, A, T, I, O, N, A, R, Y.
Stationery with an E is spelled S, T, A, T, I, O, N, E, R, Y.
For example, the delivery truck was stationary outside the office, unloading boxes of stationery.
Stationary with an A means not moving.
Stationery with an E means writing materials, like paper, pens and envelopes.
The trick is almost too easy.
Stationery with an E is for envelopes.
Stationary with an A is for a car that's parked, or at a standstill.
Our fifth and final pair is principal and principle.
Principal ending in A, L is spelled P, R, I, N, C, I, P, A, L.
Principle ending in L, E is spelled P, R, I, N, C, I, P, L, E.
For example, the school principal explained the principle behind the new phone rules.
Principal with A, L can mean the head of a school, or it can mean main, as in the principal reason.
In finance, it also means the original amount you borrowed, before interest.
Principle with L, E means a rule, a basic truth or a belief.
You might refuse to do something as a matter of principle.
Two tricks work nicely together here.
First, the principal is your pal, and pal ends in A, L.
Second, a principle is a rule, and both principle and rule end in L, E.
So why do these pairs cause so much trouble?
Mostly because we learn words by ear first, and by ear these pairs sound almost identical.
Spellcheck won't save you either, because both spellings are real words.
That's exactly why a short, silly memory trick works so well.
It gives your brain something to hold on to at the moment you're writing.
To sum up, affect is usually the action and effect is usually the result.
Use fewer for things you can count and less for amounts, money, time and distance.
And remember that a complement completes, stationery with an E is for envelopes, and the principal is your pal.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What does the memory trick RAVEN stand for?
Answer. Remember, affect is a verb, effect is a noun.
Question two. Which word goes with things you can count, fewer or less?
Answer. Fewer. Fewer cars, fewer people. Less goes with amounts, like less traffic.
Question three. How do you remember which stationery means paper and pens?
Answer. Stationery with an E is for envelopes.
That's the end of Commonly Confused Words. Nicely done. You'll never look at a supermarket sign the same way.
